lesson.title: When One Coil Talks to Another: The Physics of Mutual Inductance
lesson.summary: Mutual inductance describes how a changing current in one coil creates a magnetic field that reaches into a second, separate coil and induces a voltage there, the basic mechanism behind every transformer.
lesson.body:
Inductance, as covered earlier, describes how a coil's own changing current creates a magnetic field that pushes back against that same current, an effect confined entirely to one coil. But a changing current always creates a magnetic field that spreads out into the surrounding space, following the same right hand rule rules covered under magnetic field. If a second coil happens to sit in that space, some of that field will pass through its loops too, and by Faraday's law, a changing magnetic field through a loop induces a voltage in it. Mutual inductance is the name for this cross coil effect: current changing in coil one induces a voltage in coil two, with no wire connecting them at all.

The relationship is written as V2 = M times dI1/dt, where M is the mutual inductance in henries, the same unit as ordinary self inductance. M depends on the geometry of both coils, their number of turns, their spacing, and critically, on how much of coil one's magnetic flux actually reaches coil two rather than spreading off into open space and missing it entirely. That last factor, how efficiently the flux is shared, is what the next chapter's coupling coefficient measures directly. Mutual inductance is also symmetric: the same M describes current changing in coil two inducing voltage in coil one, written M12 = M21 = M.

Worked example: two coils have self inductances L1 = 10 millihenries and L2 = 40 millihenries, and a measurement shows their mutual inductance is M = 12 millihenries, a reasonable value for a two coil setup sharing a partial magnetic core. If the current in coil one is changing at a rate of 500 amps per second, the induced voltage in coil two is V2 = M times dI1/dt = 0.012 times 500 = 6 volts. That six volt signal in coil two exists purely because of the changing magnetic field, coil two carries no current of its own in this scenario and has no wire connection to coil one at all.

This is precisely how a transformer works: an alternating current in a primary winding creates a constantly changing magnetic field, which induces a voltage in a nearby secondary winding, transferring energy across an air gap or shared iron core without any direct electrical connection. It also means that solving a circuit with two magnetically coupled coils needs an extra term beyond simple Ohm's law and self inductance, since the voltage across each coil now depends on both its own current and the other coil's changing current.

Mutual inductance shows up in places engineers actively want it, like transformers, wireless charging pads, and RFID readers, and in places they very much do not, like unwanted crosstalk between adjacent traces on a circuit board or wires bundled too close together, where a changing signal in one wire induces unwanted noise in its neighbor.

Notice that mutual inductance, unlike simple resistance, only matters when current is changing. A transformer sitting on a steady, unchanging direct current shows no mutual effect at all, since dI1/dt is zero and V2 comes out to zero regardless of how well the two coils are aligned. This is exactly why transformers work on alternating current and are useless for stepping a steady DC voltage up or down without extra switching circuitry to chop that DC into a changing waveform first.
